claim: Shigella causes ~269 million infections and ~200,000 deaths annually, a quarter of which are of children under the age of five.
source: Shigella is a genus of Gram-negative enterobacteriaceae that causes ~269 million infections and ~200,000 deaths annually, a quarter of which are of children under the age of five (Khalil et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Khalil et al., 2018.

claim: Shigella disease symptoms include fever, abdominal cramping, and inflammatory diarrhea characterized by the presence of neutrophils and, in severe cases, blood.
source: Disease symptoms include fever, abdominal cramping, and inflammatory diarrhea characterized by the presence of neutrophils and, in severe cases, blood (Kotloff et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kotloff et al., 2018.

claim: There is no approved vaccine for Shigella.
source: There is no approved vaccine for Shigella and antibiotic resistance continues to rise (Ranjbar and Farahani, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ranjbar and Farahani, 2019.

claim: Antibiotic resistance to Shigella continues to rise.
source: There is no approved vaccine for Shigella and antibiotic resistance continues to rise (Ranjbar and Farahani, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ranjbar and Farahani, 2019.

claim: Shigella pathogenesis is believed to be driven by bacterial invasion, replication, and spread within colonic intestinal epithelial cells (IECs).
source: Shigella pathogenesis is believed to be driven by bacterial invasion, replication, and spread within colonic intestinal epithelial cells (IECs).
evidence: The claim is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Shigella virulence requires a plasmid-encoded type III secretion system (T3SS) that injects ~30 effectors into host cells.
source: Shigella virulence requires a plasmid-encoded type III secretion system (T3SS) that injects ~30 effectors into host cells (Schnupf and Sansonetti, 2019; Schroeder and Hilbi, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schnupf and Sansonetti, 2019 and Schroeder and Hilbi, 2008.

claim: The Shigella virulence plasmid encodes IcsA, a bacterial surface protein that nucleates host actin at the bacterial pole to propel the pathogen through the host cell cytosol and into adjacent epithelial cells.
source: The virulence plasmid also encodes IcsA, a bacterial surface protein that nucleates host actin at the bacterial pole to propel the pathogen through the host cell cytosol and into adjacent epithelial cells (Bernardini et al., 1989; Goldberg and Theriot, 1995).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bernardini et al., 1989 and Goldberg and Theriot, 1995.

claim: The infectious dose for Shigella in humans can be as low as 10–100 bacteria.
source: Although the infectious dose for Shigella in humans can be as low as 10–100 bacteria (DuPont et al., 1969; DuPont et al., 1989), mice are resistant to high doses of oral Shigella challenge (Freter, 1956; McGuire and Floyd, 1958).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to DuPont et al., 1969 and DuPont et al., 1989.

claim: Mice are resistant to high doses of oral Shigella challenge.
source: Although the infectious dose for Shigella in humans can be as low as 10–100 bacteria (DuPont et al., 1969; DuPont et al., 1989), mice are resistant to high doses of oral Shigella challenge (Freter, 1956; McGuire and Floyd, 1958).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Freter, 1956 and McGuire and Floyd, 1958.

claim: The Shigella T3SS inner rod (MxiI) and needle (MxiH) proteins are both potent agonists of human and mouse NAIPs.
source: Importantly, the Shigella T3SS inner rod (MxiI) and needle (MxiH) proteins are both potent agonists of human and mouse NAIPs (Reyes Ruiz et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Reyes Ruiz et al., 2017 and Yang et al., 2013.

claim: Activated NAIPs co-assemble with NLRC4 to recruit and activate the Caspase-1 (CASP1) protease.
source: Activated NAIPs then co-assemble with NLRC4 to recruit and activate the Caspase-1 (CASP1) protease (Vance, 2015; Zhao and Shao, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vance, 2015 and Zhao and Shao, 2015.

claim: CASP1 cleaves and activates the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-18 and the pore-forming protein Gasdermin-D.
source: CASP1 then cleaves and activates the pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1β and IL-18 and the pore-forming protein Gasdermin-D (Kayagaki et al., 2015; Shi et al., 2015), initiating a lytic form of cell death called pyroptosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kayagaki et al., 2015 and Shi et al., 2015.

claim: Activation of NAIP–NLRC4 in IECs mediates the cell-intrinsic expulsion of infected epithelial cells from the intestinal monolayer.
source: We and others recently demonstrated that activation of NAIP–NLRC4 in IECs further mediates the cell-intrinsic expulsion of infected epithelial cells from the intestinal monolayer (Rauch et al., 2017; Sellin et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rauch et al., 2017 and Sellin et al., 2014.

claim: It is generally accepted that inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis of infected macrophages promotes Shigella pathogenesis by initiating inflammation and by releasing bacteria from macrophages.
source: In the context of Shigella infection, it is generally accepted that inflammasome-mediated pyroptosis of infected macrophages promotes pathogenesis by initiating inflammation, and by releasing bacteria from macrophages, allowing the bacteria to invade the basolateral side of intestinal epithelial cells (Ashida et al., 2014; Lamkanfi and Dixit, 2010; Schnupf and Sansonetti, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ashida et al., 2014, Lamkanfi and Dixit, 2010, and Schnupf and Sansonetti, 2019.

claim: The Shigella T3SS effector OspC3 inhibits cytosolic LPS sensing by the human Caspase-4 (CASP4) inflammasome.
source: The Shigella T3SS effector OspC3 inhibits cytosolic LPS sensing by the human Caspase-4 (CASP4) inflammasome, but is reported not to bind to the mouse ortholog, Caspase-11 (CASP11) (Kobayashi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kobayashi et al., 2013.

claim: OspC3 is reported not to bind to the mouse ortholog of CASP4, Caspase-11 (CASP11).
source: The Shigella T3SS effector OspC3 inhibits cytosolic LPS sensing by the human Caspase-4 (CASP4) inflammasome, but is reported not to bind to the mouse ortholog, Caspase-11 (CASP11) (Kobayashi et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kobayashi et al., 2013.

claim: Infection with wild-type Shigella flexneri strain 2457T but not the avirulent BS103 strain resulted in CASP1-dependent cell death in both mouse and human cells.
source: Infection with the wild-type (WT) Shigella flexneri strain 2457T but not the avirulent BS103 strain (which lacks the virulence plasmid) resulted in CASP1-dependent cell death in both mouse (Sandstrom et al., 2019) and human cells (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A,B and a citation to Sandstrom et al., 2019.

claim: Cell death was negligible in Shigella-infected mouse Nlrc4–/– BMMs.
source: As reported previously, cell death was negligible in Shigella-infected mouse Nlrc4–/– BMMs (Suzuki et al., 2014; Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and a citation to Suzuki et al., 2014.

claim: Shigella infection induced similar levels of cell death in WT and NLRC4–/– THP1 cells, indicating that the NAIP–NLRC4 inflammasome is not essential for Shigella-induced CASP1 activation in human cells.
source: In contrast, Shigella infection induced similar levels of cell death in WT and NLRC4–/– THP1 cells, indicating that the NAIP–NLRC4 inflammasome is not essential for Shigella-induced CASP1 activation in human cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B and represents an inference from the data.

claim: Treatment of THP1 cells with LFn-MxiH+PA ('NeedleTox'), but not PA alone, induced a CASP1- and NLRC4-dependent cell death.
source: Treatment of THP1 cells with LFn-MxiH+PA ('NeedleTox'), but not PA alone, induced a CASP1- and NLRC4-dependent cell death (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Shigella MxiH and MxiI activate human NAIP–NLRC4 in a reconstituted inflammasome assay.
source: We also confirmed that Shigella MxiH and MxiI (rod) activate human NAIP–NLRC4 in a reconstituted inflammasome assay (Reyes Ruiz et al., 2017; Tenthorey et al., 2014; Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and citations to Reyes Ruiz et al., 2017 and Tenthorey et al., 2014.

claim: WT Shigella infection did not induce pyroptosis of colchicine-treated AIM2–/– THP1 cells.
source: Interestingly, WT Shigella infection did not induce pyroptosis of colchicine-treated AIM2–/– THP1 cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: NeedleTox-induced pyroptosis was significantly reduced in cells previously infected with WT but not avirulent BS103 Shigella.
source: Interestingly, NeedleTox-induced pyroptosis was significantly reduced in cells previously infected with WT but not avirulent BS103 Shigella (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Treatment with nigericin induced cell death similarly in cells that were uninfected or infected with either WT or BS103 Shigella strains.
source: As a control, treatment with nigericin, an agonist of the NLRP3 inflammasome, induced cell death similarly in cells that were uninfected or infected with either WT or BS103 Shigella strains.
evidence: The claim is presented as a control experiment result.

claim: WT Shigella infection appears to specifically suppress activation of the human NAIP–NLRC4 inflammasome in THP1 cells.
source: Thus, WT Shigella infection appears to specifically suppress activation of the human NAIP–NLRC4 inflammasome in THP1 cells, leading us to hypothesize that NAIP–NLRC4 activation may be a mouse-specific mechanism of resistance to shigellosis.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Antibiotic pre-treatment followed by oral infection allows for robust Shigella colonization of the intestinal lumen and feces compared to water-only controls.
source: Thus, to overcome this barrier, we pretreated B6 WT mice orally with streptomycin antibiotic. Consistent with prior studies, we found that antibiotic pre-treatment followed by oral infection allows for robust Shigella colonization of the intestinal lumen and feces compared to water-only controls (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: High lumenal bacterial loads (>108 CFU/g feces) did not cause overt disease in antibiotic-pretreated B6 WT mice.
source: However, these high lumenal bacterial loads (>108 CFU/g feces) did not cause overt disease (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: B6 WT and Casp1/11–/– mice were similarly resistant to Shigella infection, showing no signs of intestinal inflammation or disease.
source: In contrast, B6 WT and Casp1/11–/– mice were similarly resistant to Shigella infection, showing no signs of intestinal inflammation or disease (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: Neither CASP1 nor CASP11 are essential for resistance to Shigella in the mouse intestine.
source: Thus, neither of the primary caspases associated with the canonical or non-canonical inflammasome are essential for resistance to Shigella in the mouse intestine.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing resistance in Casp1/11–/– mice.

claim: Shigella-infected ∆Naip but not WT mice exhibited clear signs of disease at 2 days post-challenge.
source: Remarkably, Shigella-infected ∆Naip but not WT mice exhibited clear signs of disease (Figure 2). At 2 days post-challenge, ∆Naip mice had altered stool consistency (Figure 2A), cecum shrinkage, and thickening of the cecum and colon tissue (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Histological analysis of ∆Naip mice revealed edema, epithelial hyperplasia, epithelial sloughing, and inflammatory infiltrate (predominantly neutrophils and mononuclear cells in the submucosa and mucosa) exclusively in ∆Naip mice.
source: Histological analysis of primary sites of infection (cecum, colon) revealed edema, epithelial hyperplasia, epithelial sloughing, and inflammatory infiltrate (predominantly neutrophils and mononuclear cells in the submucosa and mucosa) exclusively in ∆Naip mice (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: No indicators of inflammation were observed in ∆Naip mice infected with the avirulent BS103 strain.
source: In contrast, we did not observe any indicators of inflammation in ∆Naip mice infected with the avirulent BS103 strain (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Fecal MPO from ∆Naip mice dramatically increased following Shigella infection.
source: Following Shigella infection, however, fecal MPO from ∆Naip mice dramatically increased (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: MPO levels remained low in both B6 WT and Casp1/11–/– mice or ∆Naip mice infected with the avirulent BS103 strain.
source: In contrast, MPO levels remained low in both B6 WT and Casp1/11–/– mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D) or ∆Naip mice infected with the avirulent BS103 strain (Figure 2E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: NAIP–NLRC4-deficient mice experience robust neutrophilic infiltrate consistent with human shigellosis.
source: These results indicate that NAIP–NLRC4-deficient mice experience robust neutrophilic infiltrate consistent with human shigellosis.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the MPO data and comparison to human disease.

claim: Shigella-infected B6.Nlrc4–/– mice but not B6.Nlrc4+ littermates or co-housed mice exhibited thickening of the intestinal mucosa, cecum shrinkage, increased fecal MPO levels, and acute weight loss.
source: Consistent with our prior results in ∆Naip mice, we observed thickening of the intestinal mucosa (Figure 3A), cecum shrinkage (Figure 3A,B), increased fecal MPO levels (Figure 3C), and acute weight loss (Figure 3D) in Shigella-infected B6.Nlrc4–/– mice but not B6.Nlrc4+ littermates or co-housed mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A-D.

claim: B6.Nlrc4–/– mice had diarrhea, which was apparent by visual inspection of lumenal contents and quantified by the wet-to-dry ratio of fecal pellets.
source: B6.Nlrc4–/– mice also had diarrhea, which was apparent by visual inspection of lumenal contents and quantified by the wet-to-dry ratio of fecal pellets (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: B6.Nlrc4–/– mice phenocopy the disease susceptibility of B6.∆Naip mice.
source: Thus, B6.Nlrc4–/– mice phenocopy the disease susceptibility of B6.∆Naip mice, and strongly suggest that the NAIP–NLRC4 inflammasome mediates the resistance of mice to Shigella infection.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the comparison of disease phenotypes between the two mouse strains.

claim: The NAIP–NLRC4 inflammasome mediates the resistance of mice to Shigella infection.
source: Thus, B6.Nlrc4–/– mice phenocopy the disease susceptibility of B6.∆Naip mice, and strongly suggest that the NAIP–NLRC4 inflammasome mediates the resistance of mice to Shigella infection.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data from multiple mouse strains.

claim: IL-18 levels were similarly elevated in B6.Nlrc4+ and B6.Nlrc4–/– mice relative to uninfected mice.
source: IL-18 levels were similarly elevated in B6.Nlrc4+ and B6.Nlrc4–/– mice relative to uninfected mice (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: IL-1β and KC levels were significantly elevated in B6.Nlrc4–/– relative to B6.Nlrc4+ and uninfected mice.
source: By contrast, IL-1β and KC levels were significantly elevated in B6.Nlrc4–/– relative to B6.Nlrc4+ and uninfected mice (Figure 3F), consistent with the neutrophilic inflammation observed by histology and fecal MPO ELISAs.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: There was no significant difference in the bacterial burdens of whole cecum or colon tissue between Shigella infected B6.Nlrc4+ and B6.Nlrc4–/– mice.
source: Surprisingly, despite the clear differences in disease between Shigella infected B6.Nlrc4+ and B6.Nlrc4–/– mice, we found no significant difference in the bacterial burdens of whole cecum or colon tissue (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: There was an ~20-fold difference in colonization in enriched IECs between B6.Nlrc4+ and B6.Nlrc4–/– mice.
source: We found an ~20-fold difference in colonization in enriched IECs between B6.Nlrc4+ and B6.Nlrc4–/– mice (Figure 3H), indicating that disease in our model correlates with invasion of and replication in IECs.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Disease in the mouse model correlates with invasion of and replication in IECs.
source: We found an ~20-fold difference in colonization in enriched IECs between B6.Nlrc4+ and B6.Nlrc4–/– mice (Figure 3H), indicating that disease in our model correlates with invasion of and replication in IECs.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the IEC CFU data.

claim: Shigella colonizes the intestinal tissue regardless of inflammasome activity, but can only specifically invade the epithelium and provoke disease in NAIP–NLRC4-deficient mice.
source: These data suggest that Shigella colonizes the intestinal tissue regardless of inflammasome activity, but can only specifically invade the epithelium and provoke disease in NAIP–NLRC4-deficient mice.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the CFU data from whole tissue versus IECs.

claim: 129.Nlrc4–/– mice exhibited severe signs of shigellosis, including pronounced edema, epithelial cell hyperplasia, and disruption of the columnar epithelium of infected tissues.
source: Similar to the B6 genetic background, antibiotic-pretreated 129.Nlrc4–/– but not 129.Nlrc4+/– littermates challenged with WT (or BS103) Shigella exhibited severe signs of shigellosis, including pronounced edema, epithelial cell hyperplasia, and disruption of the columnar epithelium of infected tissues (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: 129.Nlrc4–/– mice exhibited dramatic cecum shrinkage and diarrhea.
source: 129.Nlrc4–/– mice also exhibited dramatic cecum shrinkage and diarrhea (Figure 4C,D,K), lost between 8% and 18% of their starting weight within 2 days of infection (Figure 4E), and exhibited a massive increase in fecal MPO following infection (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C,D,K.

claim: 129.Nlrc4–/– mice lost between 8% and 18% of their starting weight within 2 days of infection.
source: 129.Nlrc4–/– mice also exhibited dramatic cecum shrinkage and diarrhea (Figure 4C,D,K), lost between 8% and 18% of their starting weight within 2 days of infection (Figure 4E), and exhibited a massive increase in fecal MPO following infection (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: 129.Nlrc4–/– mice exhibited a massive increase in fecal MPO following infection.
source: 129.Nlrc4–/– mice also exhibited dramatic cecum shrinkage and diarrhea (Figure 4C,D,K), lost between 8% and 18% of their starting weight within 2 days of infection (Figure 4E), and exhibited a massive increase in fecal MPO following infection (Figure 4F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: There was no significant difference in the bacterial colonization of the whole cecum and colon tissue between 129.Nlrc4+/– and 129.Nlrc4–/– mice.
source: We found no significant difference in the bacterial colonization of the whole cecum and colon tissue between 129.Nlrc4+/– and 129.Nlrc4–/– mice (Figure 4G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: IECs enriched from infected 129.Nlrc4–/– mice exhibited ~20-fold higher bacterial burdens than IECs enriched from 129.Nlrc4+/– mice.
source: However, IECs enriched from infected 129.Nlrc4–/– mice again exhibited ~20-fold higher bacterial burdens than IECs enriched from 129.Nlrc4+/– mice (Figure 4H), despite similar levels of lumenal colonization (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: 4/5 129.Nlrc4–/– mice infected with WT Shigella had occult blood in their feces.
source: Using an assay to detect occult blood (see Materials and methods), we were unable to detect blood in the feces of NAIP–NLRC4-deficient mice on the B6 background (data not shown). However, when we tested 129.Nlrc4–/– mouse stools, we found that 4/5 mice infected with WT Shigella had occult blood in their feces (Figure 4I).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: In a subsequent infection, 80% (8/10) of 129.Nlrc4–/– mice had bloody stool (occult blood only, n = 5; macroscopically visible blood, n = 3).
source: In a subsequent infection, 80% (8/10) of 129.Nlrc4–/– mice had bloody stool (occult blood only, n = 5; macroscopically visible blood, n = 3) (Figure 4J).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: 129.Nlrc4–/– mice recapitulate the bloody stool (dysentery) that is a hallmark of severe human shigellosis.
source: Thus, 129.Nlrc4–/– mice recapitulate the bloody stool (dysentery) that is a hallmark of severe human shigellosis.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation of bloody stool in 129.Nlrc4–/– mice and comparison to human disease.

claim: Shigella infected Vil1-Cre+ iNlrc4 mice, but not Cre– littermate controls, were protected from intestinal inflammation to a similar extent as co-housed Nlrc4+/– mice.
source: Shigella infected Vil1-Cre+ iNlrc4 mice, but not Cre– littermate controls, were protected from intestinal inflammation to a similar extent as co-housed Nlrc4+/– mice (Figure 5B–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5B–F.

claim: NLRC4 expression in IECs is sufficient to prevent shigellosis.
source: Thus, NLRC4 expression in IECs is sufficient to prevent shigellosis.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the protection observed in Vil1-Cre+ iNlrc4 mice.

claim: WT Shigella was not recovered from WT IEC monolayers infected with WT Shigella.
source: We were unable to recover CFUs from WT IEC monolayers infected with WT Shigella (Figure 6A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: 129.Nlrc4–/– IEC monolayers supported replication of WT Shigella.
source: In contrast, 129.Nlrc4–/– IEC monolayers supported replication of WT Shigella.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A strain lacking IcsA colonized 129.Nlrc4–/– IEC monolayers to a lesser extent than WT Shigella, consistent with loss of IcsA-mediated cell-to-cell spread.
source: The avirulent non-invasive BS103 strain was detected sporadically at low levels, independent of NAIP–NLRC4, while a strain lacking IcsA, a protein essential for Shigella actin tail formation and cell-to-cell spread (Bernardini et al., 1989; Goldberg and Theriot, 1995), colonized 129.Nlrc4–/– IEC monolayers to a lesser extent than WT Shigella, consistent with loss of IcsA-mediated cell-to-cell spread.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A and citations to Bernardini et al., 1989 and Goldberg and Theriot, 1995.

claim: Immunostaining revealed intracellular replication and actin tail formation exclusively in Nlrc4–/– IEC monolayers infected with WT Shigella.
source: Immunostaining for Shigella in infected IEC organoid cultures also revealed intracellular replication and actin tail formation (detected by fluorescent phalloidin) exclusively in Nlrc4–/– IEC monolayers infected with WT Shigella (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: IEC organotypic infections faithfully recapitulate the NAIP–NLRC4-dependent differences in Shigella replication observed in vivo.
source: Thus, IEC organotypic infections faithfully recapitulate the NAIP–NLRC4-dependent differences in Shigella replication observed in vivo.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the comparison of in vitro and in vivo data.

claim: Key Shigella virulence factors are functional within mouse cells and can initiate invasion and actin-based motility in mouse IECs, as long as the NAIP–NLRC4 inflammasome is absent.
source: In addition, our results demonstrate that key Shigella virulence factors are functional within mouse cells and can initiate invasion and actin-based motility in mouse IECs, as long as the NAIP–NLRC4 inflammasome is absent.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation of Shigella replication and actin tail formation in Nlrc4–/– IECs.

claim: There were more PI-positive cells in Shigella-infected WT versus Nlrc4–/– IEC monolayers.
source: There were more PI-positive cells in Shigella-infected WT versus Nlrc4–/– IEC monolayers (Figure 6C,E), and the average position of PI-positive cells was significantly above the monolayer (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C,E.

claim: The average position of PI-positive cells was significantly above the monolayer in Shigella-infected WT IEC monolayers.
source: There were more PI-positive cells in Shigella-infected WT versus Nlrc4–/– IEC monolayers (Figure 6C,E), and the average position of PI-positive cells was significantly above the monolayer (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The NAIP–NLRC4 inflammasome prevents Shigella invasion by coordinating the expulsion of infected IECs.
source: Thus, data from our ex vivo IEC monolayer culture system, as well as from previous work (Rauch et al., 2017), suggest that the NAIP–NLRC4 inflammasome prevents Shigella invasion by coordinating the expulsion of infected IECs.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the ex vivo data and a citation to Rauch et al., 2017.

claim: Mice infected with WT Shigella exhibited weight loss, diarrhea, increases in fecal MPO, and blood in their stool.
source: Mice infected with WT Shigella exhibited weight loss (Figure 7A), diarrhea (Figure 7B), increases in fecal MPO (Figure 7C), and blood in their stool (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A-D.

claim: Signs of disease in WT-infected mice peaked between 2 and 3 days post-infection with weight loss, stool consistency, and MPO signal returning to baseline levels at approximately seven days post-infection.
source: Signs of disease in WT-infected mice peaked between 2 and 3 days post-infection with weight loss, stool consistency, and MPO signal returning to baseline levels at approximately seven days post-infection, consistent with the disease progression and resolution of human shigellosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: 129.Nlrc4–/– mice infected with icsA mutant Shigella did not experience weight loss, diarrhea, or fecal blood, and largely phenocopied mice infected with the non-invasive BS103 strain.
source: Interestingly, 129.Nlrc4–/– mice infected with icsA mutant Shigella did not experience weight loss, diarrhea, or fecal blood, and largely phenocopied mice infected with the non-invasive BS103 strain (Figure 7A–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7A–D.

claim: A slight but significant increase in fecal MPO levels at 1–3 days post-infection was observed in 129.Nlrc4–/– mice infected with icsA mutant Shigella.
source: We did observe a slight but significant increase in fecal MPO levels at 1–3 days post-infection in these mice (Figure 7B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: icsA mutants can provoke mild inflammation upon initial colonization of the intestinal epithelium, but dissemination of bacteria among IECs is a critical driver of severe disease.
source: These results suggest that, as in humans (Coster et al., 1999; Kotloff et al., 1996), icsA mutants can provoke mild inflammation upon initial colonization of the intestinal epithelium, but that dissemination of bacteria among IECs is a critical driver of severe disease.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data and citations to Coster et al., 1999 and Kotloff et al., 1996.

claim: Regardless of the inoculum, all mice showed similar levels of lumenal colonization (>108 CFU/g feces) at one and two days post-infection.
source: Regardless of the inoculum, all mice showed similar levels of lumenal colonization (>108 CFU/g feces) at one and two days post-infection (Figure 8A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Even a relatively small bacterial population can rapidly expand within the intestines of antibiotic-treated mice.
source: This suggests that even a relatively small bacterial population can rapidly expand within the intestines of antibiotic-treated mice.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation of similar lumenal colonization regardless of inoculum.

claim: Robust disease, including weight loss, cecum shrinkage, elevated fecal MPO, and occult blood was observed in Nlrc4–/– mice regardless of the infectious dose.
source: In contrast, we observed robust disease, including weight loss, cecum shrinkage, elevated fecal MPO, and occult blood in Nlrc4–/– mice regardless of the infectious dose (Figure 8B–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8B–E.

claim: The rise in fecal MPO in mice receiving smaller inocula was delayed relative to previous infections with 5 × 107 CFU.
source: The rise in fecal MPO in mice receiving smaller inocula was delayed relative to previous infections with 5 × 107 CFU (Figure 8D, Figure 4F), suggesting that infectious dose correlates with disease onset.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8D and Figure 4F.

claim: Infectious dose correlates with disease onset.
source: The rise in fecal MPO in mice receiving smaller inocula was delayed relative to previous infections with 5 × 107 CFU (Figure 8D, Figure 4F), suggesting that infectious dose correlates with disease onset.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation of delayed MPO rise with smaller inocula.

claim: There was a 100-fold difference in bacterial colonization of IECs between Nlrc4–/– mice and Nlrc4+ mice, regardless of infectious dose.
source: Importantly, there was a 100-fold difference in bacterial colonization of IECs between Nlrc4–/– mice and Nlrc4+ mice, regardless of infectious dose, but no difference in IEC colonization among Nlrc4–/– mice inoculated with 2 × 104 – 2 × 106 CFU (Figure 8F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: There was no difference in IEC colonization among Nlrc4–/– mice inoculated with 2 × 104 – 2 × 106 CFU.
source: Importantly, there was a 100-fold difference in bacterial colonization of IECs between Nlrc4–/– mice and Nlrc4+ mice, regardless of infectious dose, but no difference in IEC colonization among Nlrc4–/– mice inoculated with 2 × 104 – 2 × 106 CFU (Figure 8F).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8F.

claim: In antibiotic treated mice, disease is fully penetrant at 2 × 104 CFU, a dose that recapitulates the infectious dose observed in at least some human patients.
source: These results indicate that in antibiotic treated mice, disease is fully penetrant at 2 × 104 CFU, a dose that recapitulates the infectious dose observed in at least some human patients.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data and comparison to human infectious dose.

claim: The NAIP–NLRC4 inflammasome is a formidable species-specific barrier to Shigella invasion of the intestinal epithelium.
source: Here, we demonstrate that the NAIP–NLRC4 inflammasome is a formidable species-specific barrier to Shigella invasion of the intestinal epithelium.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data presented.

claim: Shigella infection of antibiotic pre-treated, NAIP–NLRC4-deficient mice recapitulates key features of human shigellosis, including bacterial invasion of and replication in IECs, severe inflammatory disease at relevant sites (e.g. colon, cecum), and bloody diarrhea.
source: Shigella infection of antibiotic pre-treated, NAIP–NLRC4-deficient mice recapitulates key features of human shigellosis, including bacterial invasion of and replication in IECs, severe inflammatory disease at relevant sites (e.g. colon, cecum), and bloody diarrhea.
evidence: The claim is a summary conclusion based on all the experimental data presented.

claim: Inflammasome-deficient mice provide the first physiologically relevant mouse model of bacillary dysentery.
source: Thus, inflammasome-deficient mice provide the first physiologically relevant mouse model of bacillary dysentery.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the experimental data and comparison to previous models.

claim: Even genetically susceptible mice require oral antibiotic treatment to alter the mouse microbiome and allow Shigella to establish a replicative niche in the gut.
source: First, even genetically susceptible mice require oral antibiotic treatment to alter the mouse microbiome and allow Shigella to establish a replicative niche in the gut.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental design and observations from the study.

claim: Antibiotic pretreatment is a common practice in many mouse models of enteric bacterial infections.
source: However, this limitation is not unique to our Shigella model, as antibiotic pretreatment is a common practice in many mouse models of enteric bacterial infections (Barthel et al., 2003; Becattini et al., 2017; Bou Ghanem et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Barthel et al., 2003, Becattini et al., 2017, and Bou Ghanem et al., 2013.

claim: S. sonnei encodes a type VI secretion system that mediates competition with other bacterial species.
source: Interestingly, S. sonnei encodes a type VI secretion system that mediates competition with other bacterial species (Anderson et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Anderson et al., 2017.

claim: Interbacterial interactions may be an important selective pressure acting on Shigella in the human gut.
source: This finding suggests that interbacterial interactions may also be an important selective pressure acting on Shigella in the human gut.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the finding about S. sonnei type VI secretion system.

claim: Experimental human infection studies only variably achieved disease with 100 CFU (39%).
source: Although much is made of the low infectious dose of Shigella required to cause disease in humans, we note that experimental human infection studies only variably achieved disease with 100 CFU (39%) (DuPont et al., 1969) and even higher inocula failed to cause disease in some individuals 105–108 CFU (64%) (DuPont et al., 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to DuPont et al., 1969.

claim: Even higher inocula (105–108 CFU) failed to cause disease in some individuals (64%).
source: Although much is made of the low infectious dose of Shigella required to cause disease in humans, we note that experimental human infection studies only variably achieved disease with 100 CFU (39%) (DuPont et al., 1969) and even higher inocula failed to cause disease in some individuals 105–108 CFU (64%) (DuPont et al., 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to DuPont et al., 1989.

claim: Shigella rapidly expands in the antibiotic-treated mouse gut regardless of starting inoculum.
source: We also note that Shigella rapidly expands in the antibiotic-treated mouse gut regardless of starting inoculum, suggesting that there is a threshold dose required to establish infection, beyond which a larger inoculum may have little significance to the disease outcome.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data showing similar lumenal colonization regardless of inoculum.

claim: There is a threshold dose required to establish infection, beyond which a larger inoculum may have little significance to the disease outcome.
source: We also note that Shigella rapidly expands in the antibiotic-treated mouse gut regardless of starting inoculum, suggesting that there is a threshold dose required to establish infection, beyond which a larger inoculum may have little significance to the disease outcome.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the observation of rapid expansion regardless of inoculum.

claim: Shigella has evolved to inhibit or evade the human NAIP–NLRC4 inflammasome to limit intestinal epithelial cell death.
source: Although we do not directly address this possibility, our experiments suggest that Shigella has instead evolved to inhibit or evade the human NAIP–NLRC4 inflammasome to limit intestinal epithelial cell death.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the experimental observations.

claim: The NAIP–NLRC4 inflammasome plays a critical role in host defense by restricting Shigella replication and spread in IECs.
source: Indeed, we find that the NAIP–NLRC4 inflammasome plays a critical role in host defense by restricting Shigella replication and spread in IECs.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing increased IEC colonization in Nlrc4–/– mice.

claim: Only Nlrc4–/– but not WT IEC organoid monolayers are permissive to Shigella infection.
source: Further supporting this notion, only Nlrc4–/– but not WT IEC organoid monolayers are permissive to Shigella infection.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data from IEC organoid cultures.

claim: The data are consistent with the NAIP–NLRC4 inflammasome providing defense by coordinating the expulsion of Shigella-infected cells.
source: Our data are consistent with the NAIP–NLRC4 inflammasome providing defense by coordinating the expulsion of Shigella-infected cells.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing cell expulsion.

claim: Salmonella infected IECs are expelled from the intestinal epithelial barrier in an NLRC4-dependent manner.
source: Similarly, Salmonella infected IECs are expelled from the intestinal epithelial barrier in an NLRC4-dependent manner (Rauch et al., 2017; Sellin et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rauch et al., 2017 and Sellin et al., 2014.

claim: Epithelial inflammasomes coordinate the expulsion of infected IECs as a general defense strategy against enteric bacterial pathogens.
source: Thus, epithelial inflammasomes coordinate the expulsion of infected IECs as a general defense strategy against enteric bacterial pathogens.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the data from this study and previous work on Salmonella.

claim: In Nlrc4–/– mice, IL-1β and KC levels in target tissues are elevated, indicating that Shigella may encounter multiple inflammasomes at distinct stages of infection with opposing consequences for bacterial replication and host pathogenesis.
source: Interestingly, in Nlrc4–/– mice, IL-1β and KC levels in target tissues are elevated, indicating that Shigella may encounter multiple inflammasomes at distinct stages of infection with opposing consequences for bacterial replication and host pathogenesis.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the cytokine data from Nlrc4–/– mice.

claim: Bloody diarrhea is only observed in Nlrc4–/– mice generated on the 129 genetic background.
source: We only observe bloody diarrhea in Nlrc4–/– mice generated on the 129 genetic background.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental observations comparing B6 and 129 backgrounds.

claim: 129 mice naturally harbor a null Casp11 allele.
source: 129 mice naturally harbor a null Casp11 allele (Kayagaki et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kayagaki et al., 2011.

claim: Both the NAIP–NLRC4 and the CASP11 inflammasomes may mediate protection in IECs against Shigella invasion.
source: Although other genetic differences may contribute to the variation in susceptibility to Shigella between B6 and 129 NAIP–NLRC4-deficient mice, we speculate that both the NAIP–NLRC4 and the CASP11 inflammasomes mediate protection in IECs against Shigella invasion.
evidence: The claim is a speculation based on the differences between B6 and 129 backgrounds.

claim: The susceptibility of B6 NAIP–NLRC4-deficient (but CASP11+) mice, as well as the resistance of Casp1/11–/– mice, suggest that these inflammasomes are not strictly redundant and that NAIP–NLRC4 alone is sufficient to confer resistance to shigellosis in mice.
source: However, the susceptibility of B6 NAIP–NLRC4-deficient (but CASP11+) mice, as well as the resistance of Casp1/11–/– mice, suggest that these inflammasomes are not strictly redundant and that NAIP–NLRC4 alone is sufficient to confer resistance to shigellosis in mice.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the comparison of different mouse strains.

claim: IEC-expressed CASP4 provides protection against other human bacterial pathogens.
source: The Shigella effector OspC3 antagonizes the human LPS sensor CASP4 (Kobayashi et al., 2013), and IEC-expressed CASP4 provides protection against other human bacterial pathogens (Holly et al., 2020; Knodler et al., 2014), underscoring the importance of the LPS-sensing pathway during human infection.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Holly et al., 2020 and Knodler et al., 2014.

claim: The finding that Shigella appears to suppress the human NAIP–NLRC4 inflammasome implies that evasion and/or antagonism of inflammasomes is a general virulence strategy during human infections.
source: Similarly, our finding that Shigella appears to suppress the human NAIP–NLRC4 inflammasome implies that evasion and/or antagonism of inflammasomes is a general virulence strategy during human infections.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the experimental observations of inflammasome suppression.

claim: There is currently no licensed Shigella vaccine.
source: There is currently no licensed Shigella vaccine, and very limited knowledge of what vaccine-induced immune responses would be desirable to elicit to mediate protection (Barry et al., 2013; Mani et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Barry et al., 2013 and Mani et al., 2016.

claim: There is very limited knowledge of what vaccine-induced immune responses would be desirable to elicit to mediate protection against Shigella.
source: There is currently no licensed Shigella vaccine, and very limited knowledge of what vaccine-induced immune responses would be desirable to elicit to mediate protection (Barry et al., 2013; Mani et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Barry et al., 2013 and Mani et al., 2016.

claim: NAIP–NLRC4 inflammasome-deficient mice clear the attenuated Shigella icsA strain.
source: Our finding that NAIP–NLRC4 inflammasome-deficient mice clear the attenuated Shigella icsA strain, derivatives of which are currently deployed in human vaccine trials (Collins et al., 2008; Coster et al., 1999; Ranallo et al., 2014), speaks to the readiness of our model to support testing and development of Shigella therapeutics.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data showing clearance of icsA mutant.

claim: Derivatives of the icsA strain are currently deployed in human vaccine trials.
source: Our finding that NAIP–NLRC4 inflammasome-deficient mice clear the attenuated Shigella icsA strain, derivatives of which are currently deployed in human vaccine trials (Collins et al., 2008; Coster et al., 1999; Ranallo et al., 2014), speaks to the readiness of our model to support testing and development of Shigella therapeutics.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Collins et al., 2008, Coster et al., 1999, and Ranallo et al., 2014.

claim: Inflammasomes provide an important species-specific barrier against infection.
source: More broadly, our results also provide a striking example of how inflammasomes provide an important species-specific barrier against infection.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion based on the overall findings of the study.
